lead: A sensor responds to a physical quantity — heat, light, pressure, motion — and a transducer inside it converts that response into an electrical signal. That signal is usually weak, noisy and not linear, so a signal conditioner shapes it before an ADC reads it. An IoT device lives or dies by this chain: a badly chosen sensor sends confident but wrong data to the cloud. This chapter names the parts, classifies the sensor families, and gives the characteristics — range, accuracy, resolution, hysteresis, drift, time constant — that tell you how far the output can be trusted.
prereq: You need: Unit 1, for where a sensor sits inside an IoT device, and the device block picture in 2.3.

blocks.text: A sensor responds to a physical quantity. A transducer converts energy from one form to another — here from the physical form to electrical. A thermistor is both: it turns temperature into resistance. A signal conditioner makes the raw output usable by amplifying, filtering, linearising, and converting resistance or capacitance into a voltage or a 4–20 mA current. Without it, the ADC in 2.4 reads noise.

items: Active or passive: an active sensor needs an external supply (a strain gauge in a bridge); a passive one generates its own signal (a piezoelectric crystal, a thermocouple).
Primary or secondary: a primary sensor reacts directly to the quantity (a mercury thermometer); a secondary sensor uses a primary to give an electrical output.
Analog or digital: analog is a continuous voltage; digital is pulses or a serial word, as in a DS18B20 temperature chip.

blocks.text: Mechatronics draws the device as modules: sensing, processing, actuation and drive, joined by signal flow in one direction and power flow in the other. The sensor starts the signal chain; the actuator (2.2) ends it.
Static characteristics describe the sensor when the input is steady or changing slowly. They are what a datasheet quotes.

items: Range: the lowest and highest input it measures, say 0–100 °C, so the input span is xmax − xmin = 100 °C. The output span is ymax − ymin, for example 4–20 mA giving 16 mA.
Accuracy: closeness of the reading to the true value, quoted as ±0.5 °C or as a percentage of span.
Precision: how closely repeated readings agree with each other, not with the truth.
Resolution: the smallest input change that produces a detectable output change.
Linearity: the ideal output is a straight line; linearity error is the largest departure from it, as a percentage of span.
Hysteresis: the output at one input differs on the rising path and the falling path.
Repeatability: the spread of readings over repeated identical runs in the same direction.
Drift: slow change of output with time or ambient temperature when the input is fixed.
Dead band and threshold: an input band that gives no output change, and the smallest input that gives any output at all.
Loading effect: the measuring circuit draws current and pulls the reading down.

blocks.where: S is the sensitivity, in output units per input unit (e.g. mA/°C); Δy is the change in output; Δx is the change in input.

blocks.text: Static data never says how fast a sensor follows a change. Dynamic characteristics do.

items: Zero order: the output follows instantly, with no delay. A potentiometer is close to this.
First order: one energy-storing element, usually thermal mass, described by a time constant τ in seconds.

Second order: mass and spring, as in an accelerometer, described by the undamped natural frequency ωₙ in rad/s and the damping ratio ζ, which has no unit. ζ < 1 gives overshoot and ringing, ζ = 1 is critical damping (fastest settle without overshoot), and ζ > 1 is sluggish (overdamped).

Rise time: time to go from 10% to 90% of the final value. Settling time: time to stay inside a band, often ±2%, of the final value. Bandwidth: the highest frequency the sensor still follows at 70.7% (−3 dB) of its low-frequency output.

blocks.where: y(t) is the output at time t in seconds after a step; y_final is the steady value it settles to; τ is the time constant in seconds. At t = τ the output is 63.2% of y_final; at t = 5τ it is within 1%.

items: Resistive: a potentiometer for displacement; a strain gauge, where the gauge factor GF = (ΔR/R)/(ΔL/L) is about 2 for metal foil; an RTD of platinum, nearly linear, with a temperature coefficient of about 0.00385 Ω per Ω per °C (that is 0.385% per °C, so a 100 Ω Pt100 element changes by about 0.385 Ω per °C); a thermistor, large but non-linear.
Capacitive: C = εA/d, where ε is permittivity, A is plate area and d is the gap. Change A, d or ε to measure displacement, pressure or level.
Inductive: the LVDT slides a core between one primary and two secondary coils and gives an AC output proportional to displacement; an eddy-current sensor sees a metal target without touching it.
Resonant: a quartz crystal vibrates at a very stable frequency that shifts with temperature or pressure.

Optical: an LDR drops in resistance with light; a photodiode gives a current with a responsivity in A/W; a phototransistor gives a larger current. Vision, laser and fibre-optic sensing extend this — only a few universities go past the principle.
Solid state: a Hall sensor gives a voltage proportional to magnetic field; MEMS etches tiny beams and masses on silicon for accelerometers and gyroscopes.

Piezoelectric: charge under stress, used for vibration, knock and impact. Ultrasonic: send a pulse, time the echo, and distance d = v t / 2, with v the speed of sound in m/s and t the round-trip time in s.

figure.caption: Sensor families grouped by the electrical property they change; the resistive branch covers strain gauges, RTDs and thermistors. Piezoelectric, ultrasonic and solid-state sensors are the remaining families in the last section.

spec.aria: A tree of four sensor families — resistive, capacitive, inductive and optical — each labelled with the quantities it usually measures.

examples.question: A transmitter gives 4–20 mA for 0–100 °C. (a) Find the span and the sensitivity in mA/°C. (b) What temperature does 12.00 mA show? (c) At 60 °C the rising reading is 13.60 mA and the falling reading is 13.68 mA; find the hysteresis in mA and in °C.
steps: Output range: 4 mA at 0 °C and 20 mA at 100 °C.
Span = 20 − 4 = 16 mA over an input span of 100 − 0 = 100 °C.
For 12.00 mA, the output above the live zero is 12.00 − 4 = 8.00 mA.
Hysteresis in mA = falling − rising = 13.68 − 13.60 = 0.08 mA.
examples.answer: Span 16 mA, sensitivity 0.16 mA/°C, 12.00 mA corresponds to 50.0 °C, and the hysteresis is 0.08 mA = 0.5 °C.
examples.check:
I_min, I_max = 4.0, 20.0
T_min, T_max = 0.0, 100.0
span = I_max - I_min
sens = span / (T_max - T_min)
print(round(span, 2))
print(round(sens, 2))
print(round((12.00 - I_min) / sens, 1))
rise, fall = 13.60, 13.68
print(round(fall - rise, 2))
print(round((fall - rise) / sens, 2))

traps: Accuracy, precision and resolution are three different things. A reading can be precise (repeats well) and still inaccurate (far from truth), and a high sensitivity does not by itself improve resolution.
A transducer is the converter inside a measuring system. The instrument adds the conditioner, the ADC and the display; do not call the whole box a transducer.

Active and passive reverse meaning between books: in IoT texts an active sensor needs external power, while in instrumentation an active transducer generates its own signal. State which convention you use.
Hysteresis quoted in mA must be divided by the sensitivity to become °C. Mixing the two units is the commonest lost mark in this question.
A first-order sensor reaches 63.2% of the final value in one time constant — not 50%, and not 100%.
The 4 mA live zero sits at the bottom of the range; forgetting to subtract it shifts every temperature by 25 °C.

quiz.q: Define sensor and transducer in one line each.
quiz.a: A sensor responds to a physical quantity and gives a usable output; a transducer converts energy from one form to another, here from the physical form to an electrical signal.

quiz.q: What does the time constant τ of a first-order sensor mean numerically?
quiz.a: It is the time in which the output reaches 63.2% of its final value after a step input; after 5τ it is within 1%.

quiz.q: Why does an LVDT give an AC output, and how is the direction of the core movement known?
quiz.a: The core changes the coupling between the primary and the two secondary coils, so the secondaries carry AC voltages. They are connected in series opposition, so the amplitude gives the displacement and the phase gives its direction.

quiz.q: A sensor is quoted as ±0.5% of span on a 0–200 kPa range. Explain what that means and compute the error in kPa.
quiz.a: Any reading may be off by 0.5% of the 200 kPa span, that is 0.005 × 200 = 1.0 kPa, anywhere in the range.

quiz.q: A metal foil strain gauge has gauge factor 2.0 and is strained by 500 microstrain. Find ΔR/R as a fraction and as a percentage.
quiz.a: ΔR/R = GF × strain = 2.0 × 500 × 10⁻⁶ = 1.0 × 10⁻³, which is 0.1%. A 350 Ω gauge therefore changes by 0.35 Ω, so a bridge and amplifier are needed.

quiz.q: A pressure sensor gives 0–5 V for 0–200 kPa. Find the sensitivity, and the pressure when the output is 3.00 V.
quiz.a: Sensitivity = 5 V / 200 kPa = 0.025 V/kPa. Pressure = 3.00 / 0.025 = 120 kPa.

quiz.q: An accelerometer with damping ratio ζ = 0.2 measures a step change, and the IoT node samples it every 100 ms. Explain what the node records and why settling time decides the sampling rate.
quiz.a: With ζ well below 1 the output overshoots the true value and rings before settling, so early samples read high. The node must wait for the settling time (to within its accuracy band) before trusting a sample; sampling faster than that records the ringing, not the signal. A damping ratio closer to 0.7, or a slower sample rate, fixes it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is moving sensors onto silicon: MEMS accelerometers and gyroscopes in phones, Hall and magnetoresistive sensors in motor drives, and printed or flexible sensors on packaging. Energy-harvesting and self-powered sensors remove the battery from a node that must last ten years. Sensor fusion — combining an accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer — is where the accuracy actually comes from. In research, look for digital sensors with on-chip linearisation, and for calibration drift in cheap gas and humidity sensors. Words to search next: gauge factor, LVDT, responsivity, MEMS, sensor fusion.
